name: 長命うどん 弁天通店 (Chomei Udon Bentendori)

claims.text: Wheat is the primary ingredient (udon noodles); cross-contamination is inherent and unavoidable throughout the kitchen.
Broth is seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned in any source.
Fish-based dashi is used in the broth; tempura includes seafood toppings. No plant-based broth option is available.

name: 中華そば 白壁 あおい (Chuka Soba Shirakabe Aoi)

claims.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat; this restaurant uses shoyu tare in its broth and no tamari or wheat-free alternative is mentioned anywhere.
All broth is animal-based (chicken, pork, beef, and bonito); no plant-based cooking zone exists in this tiny 8-seat counter kitchen.

name: 中華旬菜 雲の上 (Chuuka Shunsai Kumo no Ue)

claims.text: No information on cross-contamination controls. The kitchen is small (12 seats implies a very compact cooking space) and serves wheat noodles and wheat-thickened sauces as core menu items — shared cookware and high cross-contact risk should be assumed.
Standard wheat-based soy sauce is almost certainly in use throughout the menu; ankake sauces are wheat-thickened; no tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned anywhere.
Oyster sauce, seafood stock, and egg are core components across multiple dishes; no separation between vegan and non-vegan prep is indicated.
No allergy-handling policy or allergen menu has been documented publicly. Given the small, owner-operated format, direct inquiry by phone (070-1652-0808) before visiting is the only reliable path.
Owner-chef format means the person who cooked at a top hotel Cantonese kitchen is in the room — direct communication about ingredients is more feasible than at chain restaurants.
100% rice-flour stand — no wheat, oats or buckwheat used, and even the cream is rice-flour based, so wheat cross-contact is inherently minimal. No formal celiac protocol published.
Butter, dairy custard cream, cheese and egg are used; not a vegan kitchen.
A wheat-allergic reviewer said she felt able to ask staff about ingredients and ate confidently.
Batter AND custard cream are 100% rice flour; explicitly no wheat, oats or buckwheat.
Rice-farmer-run using the family's own Hokkaido ゆめぴりか rice.
Tempura is the restaurant's core offering; shrimp, fish, and vegetables are fried together in shared oil. Cross-contamination with shellfish and wheat is inherent and unavoidable.

Standard Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat) is the expected base for tempura dipping sauce (tentsuyu) and any seasoning used at this izakaya. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternatives have been mentioned.
Shrimp and fish are fried in the same oil as vegetable tempura; miso soup served with lunch sets likely uses katsuobushi (bonito) dashi. No vegan-separated preparation has been reported.
No information about allergy handling, allergen menus, or staff training for dietary restrictions was found across any source reviewed.
Dinner is reservation-only and the small team takes each order seriously; advance reservation provides an opportunity to communicate dietary needs directly to the cook before arrival.

No dedicated gluten-free protocols or kitchen separation is documented. As a traditional kappo kitchen, wheat-containing soy sauce is a near-universal base ingredient across sauces, braises, and marinades, making cross-contamination a realistic concern.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu, which contains wheat) is the expected foundation of this cuisine style. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternatives are mentioned on any source.
Fish-based dashi (likely katsuobushi) is a foundational element of kappo cooking. Seafood and animal proteins are present throughout service. No vegan cross-contact controls are documented.

The chef has stated guests should 'speak up casually if there's something they'd like to eat,' suggesting some willingness to accommodate requests, but no formal allergy protocol or allergen menu is documented on any platform.

Owner-chef format with direct counter interaction means dietary needs can be communicated personally to the person preparing the food, which is more reliable than communicating through front-of-house staff in a large restaurant.

name: フジヤマ55 金シャチ横丁店 (Fujiyama 55 Kinshachi Yokocho)

claims.text: The entire kitchen is built around wheat-based noodles made fresh on-site daily; cross-contamination with gluten is certain and unavoidable.
Broths combine pork bone, chicken, and fish dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is almost certainly used in seasoning tare — no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned anywhere.

Every broth on the menu contains pork bone, chicken stock, and/or fish dashi (bonito, mackerel, horse mackerel). There is no plant-based alternative and shared cooking equipment makes vegan cross-contact unavoidable.
No allergy menu, allergy statement, or staff allergy protocol is published by the restaurant or venue. Diners with serious allergies should call ahead: 052-212-7375.
Noodles are made with only three ingredients (wheat flour, kansui, potato starch) and zero preservatives or additives, which simplifies the ingredient picture even if it does not remove wheat.
Mixed-fry (フライ) dishes appear on the menu, strongly suggesting shared frying oil. No dedicated fryer is mentioned.
Standard izakaya kitchen; wheat-containing soy sauce is used throughout Japanese pub cooking and no tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is noted anywhere.
Fish-forward kitchen; dashi from katsuobushi (bonito) or niboshi is standard across hot dishes, soups, and simmered items. No plant-based alternatives noted.
Non-smoking throughout the entire venue — a comfort for sensitive diners.
